title: The Definite Past Time Trap (Present Perfect vs Simple Past)
frequency: Extremely High (Appears in 80%+ of State Exams)
explanation: Present Perfect ('has/have + V3') connects a past action to the present moment. Therefore, it is GRAMMATICALLY FORBIDDEN to use Present Perfect with adverbs denoting finished, definite past time (such as yesterday, ago, last week, in 2021, on Monday). When a specific past time anchor is present, you MUST use Simple Past ('V2').
incorrectExample: The advocate general has argued the bail application yesterday.
correctExample: The advocate general argued the bail application yesterday.
trapRule: Definite Past Time Adverbs (yesterday, ago, last..., in [past year]) ➔ MANDATE Simple Past (V₂).

title: The 'Did + V2' Redundancy Pitfall
explanation: In English, the auxiliary 'did' already carries the simple past grammatical inflection. In negative sentences ('did not') and questions ('Did + Subject...?'), the main verb MUST remain in its base dictionary form (V1). Using a second past form (V2) creates an erroneous double-past construction.
incorrectExample: The petitioner did not submitted the requisite documents on time.
correctExample: The petitioner did not submit the requisite documents on time.
trapRule: Did / Did not + ALWAYS Base Verb (V₁). Never use V₂ after 'did'.

title: The Stative Verb Progressive Distortion
explanation: Certain English verbs express cognitive states, emotions, perceptions, or possession rather than dynamic physical activities. These 'stative verbs' (know, believe, understand, belong, possess, remember, hear, smell) resist the continuous/progressive (-ing) aspect under normal circumstances. Use Simple Present instead.
incorrectExample: The judicial registrar is knowing the procedural guidelines thoroughly.
correctExample: The judicial registrar knows the procedural guidelines thoroughly.
trapRule: Stative verbs (know, belong, understand, believe, want) take Simple Aspect, NOT Continuous.

title: The 'Since' vs 'For' Prepositional Confusion
explanation:
In Perfect and Perfect Continuous tenses, learners frequently interchange 'since' and 'for':
• 'Since' is used strictly for a specific starting POINT in time (since 9 AM, since Monday, since 2019, since childhood).
• 'For' is used for a DURATION or period of time (for 3 hours, for 5 days, for two decades).
incorrectExample: He has been serving in the High Court computer wing since five years.
correctExample: He has been serving in the High Court computer wing for five years.
trapRule: Since = Starting Point (e.g., since 2018) | For = Duration Count (e.g., for 5 years).

title: The 'By the Time' Future Perfect Mandate
explanation: When a sentence contains 'by + future time' (e.g., 'by tomorrow', 'by next month', 'by the time he arrives'), it indicates that an action will be completed prior to that future boundary. Candidates mistakenly choose Simple Future ('will complete') instead of the mandatory Future Perfect ('will have completed').
incorrectExample: The system assistant will upload all case records by 6 PM today.
correctExample: The system assistant will have uploaded all case records by 6 PM today.
trapRule: By + Future Time Benchmark ➔ MANDATES Future Perfect (will/shall have + V₃).

title: The 'Past of the Past' Double Simple Past Fallacy
explanation: When two actions happened in the past, and one was completed BEFORE the other began, the earlier action cannot remain in Simple Past. It must take Past Perfect ('had + V3') to establish the chronological sequence. The later action remains in Simple Past ('V2').
incorrectExample: The power supply failed after the clerk saved the database.
correctExample: The power supply failed after the clerk had saved the database.
trapRule: Earlier Past Action = Past Perfect ('had + V₃') | Subsequent Past Action = Simple Past ('V₂').
